newsitem.title: USA: Albright: tough first lady for U.S. diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Albright: tough first lady for U.S. diplomacy.

text.p: Madeleine Albright, who leaves on Saturday on her inaugural overseas trip as secretary of state, has created a glowing impression in Washington in just three weeks as the first woman to hold the post.
The Clinton adminstration's diplomatic star has started strongly, turning hard-boiled lawmakers into fawning allies and sweeping major media with interviews and cover stories.
She swept into office warning that though America was strong and its principles ascendant in the world, it must beware of complacency.

"If we are complacent or timid or unwilling to look beyond our borders, our citizens will not prosper and the framework of American leadership and the foundation of American security we have built could crumble with 21st Century speed," she said at her Jan. 23 swearing in ceremony.
But there has been a bittersweet side to the elevation to heightened fame and power for the Czech-born Albright.

Last week the Washington Post presented her with what she said she had not known: compelling documentation that her family was Jewish and that relatives, including three grandparents, perished in the Holocaust.

The revelation has sparked a flurry of debate on whether it was appropriate for her parents to conceal this information and whether Albright may have turned a blind eye to earlier hints she was not a Roman Catholic by birth, as she believed.
Cautious but plain-spoken, warm but tough, she became the embodiment of hard-hitting U.S. diplomacy in her previous post as ambassador to the United Nations.

"They have created a puppet show and called it a government," she once said of Haiti's military dictators during a 1994 U.N. Security Council meeting. "You can depart voluntarily and soon, or you can depart involuntarily and soon," she said in issuing the U.S. ultimatum to the junta.
And when Cuban jet fighters downed two unarmed Miami-based planes in 1996, she said, "This is not cojones, this is cowardice," using a Spanish vulgarity synonymous with bravado.

Albright will need all her toughness as secretary of state. Already she has served notice that the State Department will have the lead on foreign policy, not, as sometimes happened in the recent past, the National Security Council, the Commerce Department and the Pentagon.

Born in Prague 59 years ago, she says her political life was moulded by the diplomatic appeasement of Adolf Hitler at Munich and by the experience of bomb shelters in London where her family fled the Nazi invasion.

As an expert in eastern Europe, she made news with a leaked 1993 memo telling Clinton to initiate punitive NATO air strikes to destroy the Bosnian Serbs' heavy weapons. Many credit the memo with laying the groundwork for U.S. policy that led to bombing and then to the 1995 Balkan peace talks.

At the United Nations she had her successes but was also fiercely criticised -- especially last year when she cast the U.S. veto of a second-term for Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali while her 14 Security Council colleagues voted for him. He has since been forced out by U.S. pressure and succeeded by Kofi Annan of Ghana.
She also had to cope with mounting U.S. debt to the U.N. of more than $1 billion, which undercut her criticism of the U.N. chief for not doing enough to reform the world body.
Since becoming secretary of state she has taken the lead in trying to persuade Congress to approve a seven percent rise in State Department funding and pay the U.N. back dues.
Albright is keenly attuned to politics, an important channel in her rise to influence.
Those who know her well consider her warm and personable. But even critics admit her speeches get right to the point and are a refreshing change from the familiar diplomatic evasions.
Born Maria Jana Korbelova in Prague on May 15, 1937, she spent wartime with her family in London. She attended school in Switzerland at age 10 and acquired the name Madeleine.
Her father, a diplomat and academic, left his homeland with his family after the communist takeover in 1948 and got a teaching job in Denver, Colorado.
She attended exclusive Wellesley College in Massachusetts, and got a doctorate from Columbia University. She speaks Czech, Polish, Russian and French as well as English.
Albright joined the staff of Sen. Edmund Muskie, a Maine Democrat, in 1976 and two years later became a member of President Jimmy Carter's National Security Council staff.
She was an adviser to losing Democratic presidential candidates Walter Mondale and Michael Dukakis in the 1980s. She is divorced from Joseph Albright and has three daughters.
